citeAs: Lin, T.-Y., Maire, M., Belongie, S., Bourdev, L., Girshick, R., Hays, J., Perona, P., Ramanan, D., Zitnick, C. L., and Dollár, P. (2014). Microsoft COCO: Common Objects in Context. ECCV.
creator: Tsung-Yi Lin, Michael Maire, Serge Belongie, Lubomir Bourdev, Ross Girshick, James Hays, Pietro Perona, Deva Ramanan, C. Lawrence Zitnick, Piotr Dollár
description: A large-scale dataset for detecting and segmenting common objects in everyday scenes in their natural context. It contains 91 common object categories, with 2.5 million labeled instances in 328,000 images, and provides instance-level segmentation masks for object localization.
name: Microsoft COCO (MS COCO)
rai:annotationsPerItem: 8 workers were used for category labeling and 8 workers for instance spotting; each instance segmentation was done by a single worker and then verified by 3 to 5 workers.
rai:annotatorDemographics: Several children ranging in ages from 4 to 8 were asked to name every object they see in indoor and outdoor environments to help augment candidate categories; annotation tasks themselves were performed by crowd workers on Amazon Mechanical Turk.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: The paper analyzes annotation quality by comparing crowd workers with seven expert workers on category labeling. Ground truth was computed by majority vote of the experts; the union of 8 AMT workers achieved greater recall than any expert worker, and segmentations were also explicitly verified by multiple workers with low-quality work discarded.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotation was performed in stages: category labeling with a hierarchical super-category interface where workers dragged category icons onto one instance, instance spotting where workers marked all instances of a category, and instance segmentation where workers segmented each object instance. Workers completed training tasks for segmentation, and verification tasks were used to reject poor-quality segmentations.
rai:dataBiases: The dataset was intentionally designed to reduce bias toward iconic, canonical object views by collecting non-iconic images from Flickr using object-object and object-scene queries. The paper also notes category presence can be ambiguous because of image ambiguity or disagreement about category definitions.
rai:dataCollection: Images were collected mainly from Flickr by searching for pairwise combinations of object categories and object-scene category pairs to obtain non-iconic images with contextual relationships. Candidate images were then filtered with AMT tasks to remove invalid or iconic images, yielding 328,000 images.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: The raw data consisted of Flickr photos associated with searchable metadata and keywords, retrieved using object-object and object-scene queries; for rare cases, single-category search results were also collected and then filtered.
rai:dataCollectionType: Web Scraping, User-generated content data, Manual Human Curator
rai:dataLimitations: The 2014 release was limited to a subset of 80 categories, and segmentations were not collected for 11 categories because they had too many instances, were ambiguous and difficult to label, were confused with other categories, or had too few instances. The dataset currently labels only 'things' and not 'stuff', and crowd regions with many tightly grouped instances are ignored for evaluation.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Candidate images were explicitly filtered to remove iconic images. Near-duplicate images were detected and removed, images were grouped by photographer and date taken to reduce duplicates across splits, and in images with many instances of a category the remaining instances after 10-15 were marked as 'crowds' using a single segment.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: The collection pipeline included filtering candidate Flickr images to remove invalid or iconic images, hierarchical category labeling, near-duplicate removal using a duplicate detector, and split construction by grouping images by photographer and date taken. Tight-fitting bounding boxes were also obtained from segmentation masks for some analyses.
rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The dataset was released in stages, with the first half released in 2014 and the second half planned for 2015. The paper states that MS COCO will evolve and grow over time, that up-to-date information is available online, and that the authors are actively exploring adding various new annotations.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset is intended to advance object detection and scene understanding by providing richly annotated images of common objects in natural context. The paper does not provide an extended ethical impact discussion, but it frames the dataset as supporting practical applications and future research.
rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is intended for research on object recognition, object detection, instance segmentation, contextual reasoning, precise 2D localization, and broader scene understanding.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: Near-duplicate images were detected with the method cited as [43].
rai:personalSensitiveInformation: The dataset contains photographs of everyday scenes and includes the category 'person'; images may depict people.
